title: AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026
content:
AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026: Connecting Students with Cloud and AI On Saturday, November 21, 2026, I had the opportunity to take part in AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026, a technology event dedicated to students who are interested in Cloud Computing and Artificial Intelligence. The event took place from 9:00 AM to 11:30 AM on the 26th floor of Bitexco Financial Tower in Ho Chi Minh City.
Organized by the AWS Student Builder Groups, including AWS Cloud Club, FPTU, NEU, and PTIT, the event brought together students who share an interest in Cloud and AI technologies. It provided an opportunity to learn from experienced speakers, gain practical knowledge, and connect with the local technology community.
1. Event Overview AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026 was designed to help students get closer to the real-world applications of Cloud Computing and AI.
Rather than focusing only on theoretical knowledge, the event aimed to create an environment where students could interact with experienced professionals, explore practical technology topics, and exchange ideas with other members of the community.
Some key information about the event:
Event: AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026 Date: Saturday, November 21, 2026 Time: 9:00 AM – 11:30 AM Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City Organizers: AWS Student Builder Groups Vietnam Cost: Free admission 2. Key Highlights Learning from Experienced Speakers One of the main highlights of the event was the opportunity to gain practical knowledge about Cloud Computing and AI from experienced speakers.
For students who are beginning their journey in these fields, learning from people with real-world experience can provide a clearer understanding of how technologies are applied beyond classroom exercises and personal projects.
Connecting with the Technology Community The event also created an opportunity to meet other students who are interested in AWS, Cloud Computing, and AI.
Exchanging ideas and experiences with people from different universities can help broaden perspectives, discover new learning resources, and build connections that may be valuable in the future.
Interactive Activities and Networking In addition to the knowledge-sharing sessions, participants could take part in Q&A discussions and minigames.
These activities made the event more interactive and encouraged students to communicate, ask questions, and engage with the community. There were also exclusive gifts for participants who actively joined these activities.
3. What I Gained from the Event 1. A Better Understanding of Cloud and AI The event reinforced the importance of continuously learning about Cloud Computing and AI, two areas that are increasingly relevant to modern software development.
It also encouraged me to explore how AWS services can be used to solve practical problems rather than learning each service independently.
2. Learning Beyond the Classroom Listening to experienced speakers and interacting with the technology community provided a different perspective compared with studying through online courses or documentation alone.
I realized that practical experience and knowledge sharing are important parts of becoming a better software engineer.
3. Expanding My Professional Network Meeting students from different universities gave me the chance to exchange learning experiences and understand how others approach their Cloud and AI learning journeys.
Building connections within the technology community can also create opportunities for future collaboration and professional development.
4. Staying Motivated to Explore AWS Participating in a community event like this encouraged me to continue developing my AWS knowledge.
I want to apply what I have learned to personal projects, gain more hands-on experience, and gradually build the technical skills needed for a future career in Cloud Computing and DevOps.
5. Conclusion AWS Student Community Day Vietnam 2026 was a valuable opportunity to connect with the student technology community and explore the growing fields of Cloud Computing and AI.
The event reminded me that learning technology is not only about studying documentation or completing technical exercises. It is also about sharing knowledge, learning from experienced people, and actively participating in the community.
Moving forward, I hope to apply the knowledge gained from these experiences to my own projects and continue improving my skills in AWS, Cloud Computing, and DevOps.

title: Event 2
content:
Saturday Morning at Bitexco: Five Sessions, Three Hours, and Five Lessons to Take Away On Saturday, November 14, 2026, I attended the First Cloud AI Journey meetup on the 26th floor of Bitexco Financial Tower. The event lasted three hours, from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM, and featured five consecutive sessions covering Cloud Computing and AI Agents, presented by experienced Tech Leads and engineers working in the industry.
As a student, my main purpose was to gain practical knowledge, listen to industry professionals, and better understand how these technologies are being applied in real projects. The atmosphere was welcoming and comfortable, but whenever a live demonstration or Q&A session started, the room quickly became quiet as attendees focused on the presentations and took notes.
What I Found Most Interesting 1. Building a Vietnamese Voice AI Call Center The first session introduced how to develop a Vietnamese voice-based call center using AWS. One important point discussed was latency. Even a very short delay in voice responses can make an AI conversation feel unnatural.
The most impressive moment was a live demonstration in which an AI system made an actual phone call and conducted an initial interview for a Cloud Engineer position in Vietnamese. Its ability to communicate naturally showed me that Voice AI is no longer just an experimental concept but is becoming a practical solution for real-world applications.
2. Two Important Perspectives on Cloud Security Two sessions focused on improving infrastructure security.
The first discussed sharing resources across multiple AWS accounts within an AWS Organization. The presentation highlighted the importance of defining clear permission boundaries to ensure that users can only access the resources they are authorized to manage.
The second session introduced the concept of shifting security checks earlier into the development process. This included scanning Infrastructure as Code (IaC) during pull requests and using an adversarial user-persona agent to test staging environments before deployment.
Both sessions reinforced an important principle: identifying security problems early can significantly reduce the effort and cost required to resolve them.
3. Bringing AI Agents into Production with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Another session explored Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and how AI Agents can be operated in production environments.
I was particularly interested in the discussion about agent memory management. The speaker explained the importance of separating short-term and long-term memory so that an agent can retain useful information about users without keeping unnecessary context.
This helped me understand that building an AI Agent involves more than simply connecting a model to a set of tools. Memory management and reliable execution are also essential parts of the system.
4. Kiro Crew and the Closing Q&A This was my favorite part of the event. The session introduced the idea of running continuous AI Agents to support development activities such as code reviews and system health checks.
The closing Q&A provided several practical insights. The speakers discussed how they manage context windows, monitor token consumption across different components, remove outdated memory to control costs, and establish guardrails to prevent AI systems from accidentally deleting infrastructure or exposing sensitive information.
These discussions helped me see the importance of balancing AI automation with security, cost management, and operational control.
Five Lessons I Want to Apply After This Meetup 1. Greater Agent Autonomy Requires Stronger Security Controls Throughout the sessions, from IAM permissions to AI guardrails, the speakers repeatedly emphasized considering what could go wrong before focusing on what an AI system can accomplish.
For my personal coding-assistant project, I want to review how credentials are managed, make sure no sensitive information or secrets are stored in the repository, and limit tool permissions to only what the agent actually needs by following the Least Privilege principle.
2. Context and Memory Need to Be Managed Carefully Previously, I often included large amounts of information in AI prompts because I assumed that providing more context would always produce better results.
However, the Q&A helped me realize that unnecessarily large context windows can increase token consumption and sometimes make AI responses less focused.
Going forward, I plan to divide complex tasks into smaller steps, use separate sessions when working on different tasks, and provide only the information relevant to each specific request.
3. Security Should Be Part of the Development Process from the Beginning The discussion about detecting vulnerabilities during code reviews made me reconsider my usual development approach. I often focus on making a project work first and only think about security afterward.
I want to change this habit by checking infrastructure configurations, access permissions, and sensitive information before every deployment, including development and testing environments.
4. Learn from Engineers with Real Production Experience Listening to engineers discuss actual technical challenges helped me recognize the difference between completing classroom assignments and maintaining systems in production.
Instead of only learning concepts theoretically, I plan to choose one topic from the meetup, such as building a lightweight AI Agent with proper logging, and implement a small practical project to understand the process more deeply.
5. Become More Active in Technology Communities I am still somewhat hesitant when it comes to approaching people I have never met. However, this meetup reminded me that participating in a community is much more valuable when I actively communicate and exchange ideas with others.
For future events, I want to challenge myself to ask at least one question during the Q&A session and introduce myself to two new attendees.
Final Thoughts I left Bitexco with plenty of new information to think about. More importantly, the event helped me understand an engineering mindset that I had not fully appreciated before: getting an AI system to work is only the first step. Making it secure, cost-efficient, reliable, and manageable is what truly matters.
This week, I plan to start with two practical improvements to my current project: reviewing access permissions and removing any unnecessary secrets, as well as improving the way I organize and manage context when working with AI.
For anyone who is beginning their journey in Cloud Computing or AI, I would recommend attending technology meetups and connecting with people in the industry. Those three hours on a Saturday morning gave me valuable perspectives that would have been difficult to gain through self-study alone.
Some event photos Overall, the event not only provided technical knowledge but also helped me reshape my thinking about application design, system modernization, and cross-team collaboration.

title: Blog 1
content:
Automating Medical Coding with AWS Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Medical coding is the process of translating free-text clinical phrases such as “migrane” (misspelled) or “flutters in my chest sometimes” into standardized codes from dictionaries like MedDRA (adverse events) and WHODrug (medications). It is safety-critical—a single wrong code can route an event into the wrong safety signal—yet largely repetitive and traditionally reviewed term by term by human coders. Handing the entire workflow over to an autonomous agent makes the execution path dependent on model reasoning, making it difficult to review and reproduce.
AWS presents a reference pattern that resolves this tension by letting a deterministic workflow control the execution order while constraining the agent to make judgments inside a bounded step.
Core Architecture Components AWS Step Functions: Orchestrates the pipeline (Standard Workflow), with each execution processing a single term and preserving full execution history for auditing. AWS Lambda: Executes deterministic processing steps (CheckDirect, WriteBack, and MCP tool handlers). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness & Gateway: Runs the coding agent and exposes two MCP tools: search_dictionary and get_study_info. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector: Stores reference dictionaries and vector embeddings in a single database. Amazon Bedrock: Provides Claude Sonnet 5 for agent reasoning and Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 for semantic retrieval. Cost-Optimized Execution Flow The pipeline follows a cost-first escalation strategy—resolving simple cases with the lowest-cost deterministic mechanism before invoking an LLM:
Direct Lookup: Matches the input against predefined dictionary entries or synonym lists (via the CheckDirect Lambda function) using exact or synonym matching, resolving straightforward cases in the first step without calling an LLM. Agentic Invocation: Triggered only when direct lookup fails. The Coding Agent (running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) analyzes the term, retrieves dictionary candidates, and queries study context through MCP tools to disambiguate complex phrases. Route on Confidence Score: Decisions are routed based on the agent’s confidence score: 0.90 or higher: Automatically accept and code the term. 0.70 to below 0.90: Route to human-in-the-loop review. Below 0.70: Keep open for further review. Outcome Persistence: Before persisting data (via the WriteBack Lambda function), the system verifies that the selected code exists in the dictionary and stores the full hierarchy path alongside a concise explanation of the agent’s reasoning. Why Confidence-Based Routing Beats Raw Embedding Similarity One of the strongest aspects of this design is routing on agent confidence rather than raw embedding similarity alone:
“migrane” scored only 0.37 in embedding similarity yet 0.97 in agent confidence, whereas “flutters in my chest sometimes” scored 0.65 in similarity but only 0.75 in confidence—embedding similarity alone would have ranked these two cases in the wrong order. The identical phrase “cramps” was coded as “muscle spasms” (0.92, auto-coded) in an oncology study and “abdominal pain” (0.85, routed to human review) in a reflux study because the agent read the study description via get_study_info. Caveats & Practical Notes Reference sample only: Not validated for clinical use; requires benchmarking against a labeled ground-truth dataset to measure accuracy and auto-coding error rates before production adoption. Confidence score variance across runs: Across six runs of the oncology “cramps” case, confidence ranged from 0.75 to 0.92 (2 auto-coded, 4 routed to review), though the selected code remained identical. Testing should evaluate the chosen code and account for score variance below 0.90. Retrieval limits agent selection: Because “Palpitations” ranked 19th in retrieval, the agent never considered it. The article recommends hybrid retrieval to improve candidate recall. Licensing & compliance: MedDRA and WHODrug require commercial licenses, and handling protected health information requires signing a BAA for HIPAA-eligible AWS services. Cost driver: The largest cost component is the Aurora Serverless v2 cluster (minimum 0.5 ACU, billed even while idle); the article does not publish an exact total cost estimate. Scope boundary: This pattern is not suited for open-ended conversational workflows where the agent itself must decide arbitrary next steps. Key Takeaway I read this article to study a clean architectural separation: delegate judgment to the AI agent, while keeping execution order, confidence thresholds, and audit trails firmly under workflow control.
Source: Automate medical coding with Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Sachin Doshi, Andrei Maksimov, Rostislav Markov, AWS Architecture Blog (October 21, 2026)
Link: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/automate-medical-coding-with-step-functions-and-amazon-bedrock-agentcore/

AWS CLOUD & AI DAY 2026: HCMC WATCH PARTY When AWS Cloud & AI Day 2026 took place in Hanoi, I couldn’t fly up to attend in person. Instead, I joined the Watch Party at the AWS office in Ho Chi Minh City, hosted by the AWS Study Group community. At first, I just wanted to watch the livestream and soak in the atmosphere. As it turned out, the most valuable part of the day came from the casual conversations during the breaks.
The room was packed with over 300 builders who had set aside their daily work for the entire day. The vibe was warm and buzzed with energy every time the screen cut to an intermission, as everyone immediately turned to discuss what they had just heard.
What Stood Out Most Three Key Takeaways from the Keynote I paid close attention to three major themes: the rise of Agentic AI (where AI moves beyond answering prompts to autonomously executing multi-step workflows); the criticality of a solid data foundation as a prerequisite for real-world AI adoption; and cloud infrastructure modernization strategies for enterprises.
Real Value at the Roundtable Discussions Surprisingly, the best insights didn’t come from the main stage. During the breakout discussions, Solution Architects and developers spoke candidly about the realities of moving an AI Agent from a proof of concept (POC) into production, as well as practical ways to optimize cloud costs. Hearing practitioners share real-world roadblocks hit much harder than reading slides—I spent most of my time quietly taking notes.
4 Lessons I’m Applying to My Own Work 1. A working demo is just the starting line Listening to everyone break down real deployments made me realize how wide the gap is between an AI Agent running smoothly on a local machine and operating reliably in production. For my own small side project, I plan to add the things I previously overlooked: logging to trace the agent’s actions, tightening access permissions (least privilege), and setting up monitoring to detect when the agent makes a mistake.
2. Data defines the ceiling of what AI can do The emphasis on data foundations made me take an honest look at my current project: my data is scattered, with inconsistent naming conventions everywhere. This week, I will consolidate and standardize my dataset before even thinking about upgrading models or making the agent “smarter.”
3. Cost is an architectural concern, not an afterthought Until now, I only cared about getting things to work. The discussions showed me that serious engineers factor in costs right when drawing the architecture diagram, rather than getting shocked by the bill at the end of the month. I’m going to make a habit of estimating costs for every project—even learning ones—and comparing them against actual usage after 30 days.
4. Don’t hesitate to start a conversation at events I’m naturally hesitant to strike up conversations with strangers, but this time I pushed myself to ask a few people sitting next to me about their work. Those chats gave me far more practical perspective than grinding through documentation alone at home. My goal for future events is simple: meet at least two new people and follow up with them afterward.
Final Thoughts I walked away feeling caught up with where the industry is heading, yet my biggest takeaway was about how we learn: watching the exact same keynote alone versus watching it surrounded by a community yields two completely different experiences.
My first step this week is to audit my personal AI Agent project against those three pillars: logging, data, and cost. If you’re learning on your own and feeling stuck, try finding a local tech community—having peers to bounce ideas off makes the lessons stick much faster.

title: Blog 2
content:
Upgrading AI-Powered Game Backends with New Amazon DynamoDB Features When integrating AI into games, the hardest engineering challenge is often not choosing the model, but choosing the state-storage infrastructure. A generative NPC that forgets every prior conversation, an AI dungeon master that loses the quest storyline mid-session, or an agent that loses state after an AWS Lambda cold start all share the same root cause: the lack of a durable, globally consistent state layer.
The AWS for Games Blog post highlights that Amazon DynamoDB—already widely used in game backends for player profiles, inventories, leaderboards, and session state—now introduces four enhancements tailored for AI-powered game workloads.
Four Key Amazon DynamoDB Enhancements Multi-Region Strong Consistency (MRSC): Writes are synchronously replicated to at least one other Region before returning success, so reading with ConsistentRead=True from any replica returns the latest version. Under the hood, it uses a three-node multi-Region journal that commits once two of the three nodes confirm. The trade-off is single-digit millisecond additional latency, making it suitable for premium currency balances and agent checkpoints. Zero-ETL to Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse: DynamoDB automatically replicates table data to Lakehouse in Apache Iceberg format using incremental CDC synchronization (typically within minutes) without consuming production read capacity—replacing the traditional six-service pipeline (Streams, Lambda/Glue, S3, Glue Data Catalog, Athena). LangGraph DynamoDBSaver: Persists agent checkpoints and state (conversation history, tool outputs, NPC relationship scores, quest context) keyed by each player session’s thread_id. Payloads exceeding 350 KB are automatically offloaded to Amazon S3. Pricing Reductions: Effective November 1, 2024, on-demand throughput pricing was reduced by 50% and Global Tables replication write pricing by up to 67%. Reference Architecture Summary The blog combines all four features into a reference design:
Single-table design with partition key player_id and sort key record_type. Dedicated MRSC tables per Region set, using strong consistency (ConsistentRead=True) for premium currency and agent checkpoints, and eventual consistency for leaderboards. Zero-ETL enabled on the game-session table to retrain personalization models weekly in SageMaker Lakehouse. On-demand capacity mode with warm throughput pre-configured to 2× expected peak ahead of major in-game events. Caveats & Critical Observations MRSC feature limitations: MRSC does not support TTL, Local Secondary Indexes (LSI), or transactional operations (TransactWriteItems, TransactGetItems). Data expiration must be handled manually via conditional writes or cleanup Lambda functions. Regional-set boundary: MRSC only operates within regional sets (US, Europe, Asia-Pacific) and does not yet provide cross-continent strong consistency. Studios with global players should use MRSC per regional set and accept eventual consistency for global leaderboards. Zero-ETL prerequisites: Enabling zero-ETL requires turning on Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) on the source table and granting permissions to AWS Glue. Cost example discrepancy: The article cites 10 million writes per day across two replicas with pricing dropping from ~$1.25 to $0.625 per million WRUs, yet claims ~$6,250/month in savings. Recalculating from those exact figures yields only about $375/month, so teams should compute savings against their own actual traffic volumes. Lack of empirical benchmarks: The post describes architecture only and does not include measured latency, cost, or player-experience metrics. Diagram vs. text nuance: While the diagram refers to a “single-table design,” it marks game-session records as outside MRSC—making it most logical to interpret game-session data as residing in a separate table serving as the zero-ETL source. Key Takeaway I read this post to study a core design principle for AI in games: the quality of an NPC or AI agent’s player experience depends heavily on durable, consistent state persistence, not just the underlying model.
Source: Level up your AI-powered game backend with Amazon DynamoDB new features — Naveen Kantamneni, Jackie Jiang, AWS for Games Blog (October 21, 2026)

content:
AWS Plant Disease Detection Project Proposal Twelve week implementation and validation plan 16 October 2026 | Sydney | ap-southeast-2
We propose a twelve-week implementation and validation program for a containerized tomato leaf classification application on EC2, S3 and CloudWatch. The plan starts from the existing prototype and closes deployment, evidence and operational gaps.
1 Executive summary The project will deliver a reproducible AWS demonstration with a responsive frontend, CPU inference API, privately stored model artifacts and one operational RAM alarm. GitHub Actions will publish images; a controlled manual procedure will deploy and roll back compatible image and model versions. This scope fits a backend and MLOps learning project without requiring serverless or microservices claims.
The planning scenario uses 240 EC2 hours over twelve weeks and a gross budget of USD 67.20 including a 20 percent contingency. The account screenshot showed USD 100 available; an additional USD 100 is not assumed to be earned. Actual credit eligibility, expiry, regional prices and tax must be checked before spending. The estimate is a planning allowance, not an AWS quotation. [6–12]
2 Problem statement A locally trained classifier is difficult to reproduce on another host when model weights, class ordering, preprocessing and dependencies are managed separately. LAN-only access limits demonstrations, and an apparently healthy process may still fail prediction because of missing weights, CORS, queue saturation or permission errors. Source-code synchronization alone does not update a running container.
The project therefore needs a versioned release identity, least-privilege access to artifacts, evidence of real inference on AWS, actionable host monitoring and a documented recovery process. The current prototype supplies working components, but it does not yet establish high availability, field accuracy or automated production deployment.
3 Solution architecture AWS services used Service Role Design choice Amazon EC2 Run frontend and API containers One x86_64 host in Sydney Amazon S3 Store checkpoint and class map Private versioned artifacts Amazon CloudWatch Logs metrics dashboard and RAM alarm 60 second Agent metrics; 7 day logs IAM and VPC Identity and network controls Instance role and source IP rules Amazon SNS Deliver alarm email One confirmed email subscription Component design The browser reaches Next.js on port 3000 and FastAPI on port 8000 at the same EC2 hostname. FastAPI loads a MobileNet checkpoint once per process and validates the supplied class map. Prediction and Grad-CAM++ share a bounded execution slot. S3 is accessed at deployment time; uploaded user images do not need to be persisted in S3 for the current use case.
GitHub Actions -> GHCR -> manual deployment to EC2 Private S3 artifacts -> host version directory -> read-only API mount Browser -> Next.js frontend and FastAPI API Container logs + Agent metrics -> CloudWatch -> RAM alarm -> SNS The architecture deliberately uses a public subnet with restricted inbound access for the demonstration. S3 VPC endpoints, on-premises connectivity, DNS simulation, load balancing and autoscaling are outside the baseline. A private-network extension can be evaluated later without being reported as an implemented feature.
4 Technical implementation Build the frontend with its existing multi-stage Dockerfile and standalone Next.js output. Build the API with Dockerfile.deploy so the checkpoint remains outside the image. CI gates include Python tests, frontend build, backend build and frontend container smoke tests. Publish both images with full commit tags and record digests; tests using fixture weights remain distinct from real-model acceptance tests.
Create the EC2 instance profile with scoped GetObject permission and CloudWatch delivery permissions. Download model artifacts from mobilenet-distilled-v1 and compare SHA256 values before mounting them read-only. title: Blogs Posted
content:
Automating Medical Coding with AWS Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Medical coding is the process of translating free-text clinical phrases such as “migrane” (misspelled) or “flutters in my chest sometimes” into standardized codes from dictionaries like MedDRA (adverse events) and WHODrug (medications). It is safety-critical—a single wrong code can route an event into the wrong safety signal—yet largely repetitive and traditionally reviewed term by term by human coders. Handing the entire workflow over to an autonomous agent makes the execution path dependent on model reasoning, making it difficult to review and reproduce.
AWS presents a reference pattern that resolves this tension by letting a deterministic workflow control the execution order while constraining the agent to make judgments inside a bounded step.
Core Architecture Components AWS Step Functions: Orchestrates the pipeline (Standard Workflow), with each execution processing a single term and preserving full execution history for auditing. AWS Lambda: Executes deterministic processing steps (CheckDirect, WriteBack, and MCP tool handlers). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Harness & Gateway: Runs the coding agent and exposes two MCP tools: search_dictionary and get_study_info. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL + pgvector: Stores reference dictionaries and vector embeddings in a single database. Amazon Bedrock: Provides Claude Sonnet 5 for agent reasoning and Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 for semantic retrieval. Cost-Optimized Execution Flow The pipeline follows a cost-first escalation strategy—resolving simple cases with the lowest-cost deterministic mechanism before invoking an LLM:
Direct Lookup: Matches the input against predefined dictionary entries or synonym lists (via the CheckDirect Lambda function) using exact or synonym matching, resolving straightforward cases in the first step without calling an LLM. Agentic Invocation: Triggered only when direct lookup fails. The Coding Agent (running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) analyzes the term, retrieves dictionary candidates, and queries study context through MCP tools to disambiguate complex phrases. Route on Confidence Score: Decisions are routed based on the agent’s confidence score: 0.90 or higher: Automatically accept and code the term. 0.70 to below 0.90: Route to human-in-the-loop review. Below 0.70: Keep open for further review. Outcome Persistence: Before persisting data (via the WriteBack Lambda function), the system verifies that the selected code exists in the dictionary and stores the full hierarchy path alongside a concise explanation of the agent’s reasoning. Why Confidence-Based Routing Beats Raw Embedding Similarity One of the strongest aspects of this design is routing on agent confidence rather than raw embedding similarity alone:
“migrane” scored only 0.37 in embedding similarity yet 0.97 in agent confidence, whereas “flutters in my chest sometimes” scored 0.65 in similarity but only 0.75 in confidence—embedding similarity alone would have ranked these two cases in the wrong order. The identical phrase “cramps” was coded as “muscle spasms” (0.92, auto-coded) in an oncology study and “abdominal pain” (0.85, routed to human review) in a reflux study because the agent read the study description via get_study_info. Caveats & Practical Notes Reference sample only: Not validated for clinical use; requires benchmarking against a labeled ground-truth dataset to measure accuracy and auto-coding error rates before production adoption. Confidence score variance across runs: Across six runs of the oncology “cramps” case, confidence ranged from 0.75 to 0.92 (2 auto-coded, 4 routed to review), though the selected code remained identical. Testing should evaluate the chosen code and account for score variance below 0.90. Retrieval limits agent selection: Because “Palpitations” ranked 19th in retrieval, the agent never considered it. The article recommends hybrid retrieval to improve candidate recall. Licensing & compliance: MedDRA and WHODrug require commercial licenses, and handling protected health information requires signing a BAA for HIPAA-eligible AWS services. Cost driver: The largest cost component is the Aurora Serverless v2 cluster (minimum 0.5 ACU, billed even while idle); the article does not publish an exact total cost estimate. Scope boundary: This pattern is not suited for open-ended conversational workflows where the agent itself must decide arbitrary next steps. Key Takeaway I read this article to study a clean architectural separation: delegate judgment to the AI agent, while keeping execution order, confidence thresholds, and audit trails firmly under workflow control.
Source: Automate medical coding with Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — Sachin Doshi, Andrei Maksimov, Rostislav Markov, AWS Architecture Blog (October 21, 2026)

title: Blog 3
content:
Resolving Security Signals Faster with Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Agentic SOC Security teams rarely suffer from a shortage of alerts—they suffer from a shortage of triage capacity. Detection tools generate far more alerts than human analysts can investigate, and the same signal can mean completely different things depending on the environment: a password-guessing pattern might be an authorized penetration test in one account and an active credential-stuffing attack in another. Amazon GuardDuty flags unusual API activity, but does not tell you whether it is a real incident, a misconfiguration, or authorized testing.
This AWS Marketplace Blog post (co-authored with two writers from Arctic Wolf) explains how Arctic Wolf combines AI agents with its Concierge Security Team to turn raw AWS security findings into actionable decisions.
Core Architecture Components Aurora Agentic SOC: An AI-agent-driven security operations center built on the Aurora Superintelligence platform. Swarm of Experts: An agentic framework of specialized agents collaborating on triage, investigation, and response, with human analysts validating and taking over escalated cases. Concierge Security Team: Dedicated human specialists who understand the customer’s environment and act on their behalf. AWS Security Hub CSPM: Aggregates findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie, AWS Config, and third-party tools into the standardized ASFF format. Amazon EventBridge + Amazon Data Firehose + Amazon S3 + AWS Lambda: An event-driven ingestion pipeline forwarding findings directly to the SOC. AWS CloudFormation: Templates provided by Arctic Wolf to deploy the entire ingestion pipeline inside the customer’s AWS account. Event-Driven Ingestion Flow The ingestion pipeline operates without polling—findings are pushed immediately as they appear:
AWS Security Hub CSPM normalizes incoming findings into ASFF. Amazon EventBridge emits an event whenever a new finding arrives. Amazon Data Firehose buffers and streams events into a landing S3 bucket, handling sudden incident spikes smoothly. AWS Lambda processes, enriches, and delivers the records into the destination S3 bucket. Arctic Wolf SOC reads the destination bucket via cross-account IAM delegation (no polling) and correlates findings with endpoint, network, and identity telemetry in Aurora. Beyond Security Hub, Arctic Wolf integrates with AWS CloudTrail, Amazon GuardDuty (single-account or multi-account via AWS Organizations / Control Tower), and AWS WAF, with over 120 alert rules reported across these integrations.
Human-Agent Division of Labor What stands out most is placing AI agents and humans in the roles where each excels: AI agents perform large-scale initial triage and correlation, while human experts handle complex judgment calls and customer communication. According to customer CloudHesive (cited in the post), reported outcomes included 50% fewer alerts requiring triage, 99% faster investigation-to-remediation, and 10× cost savings compared to the estimated cost of building an in-house SOC.
Caveats & Practical Notes Vendor-authored metrics: Because the article is co-authored by Arctic Wolf staff and closes with a subscription call-to-action, claims such as 10,000+ customers, 10+ trillion events per week, 14+ years of telemetry, and a 4.9/5 Gartner Peer Insights rating are vendor-provided without independent verification. Self-reported customer results: CloudHesive’s figures are customer-reported, and the 10× savings comparison is measured against an estimated in-house build cost rather than actual spend. Escalation logic not detailed: The article states that agents know when to stop and escalate to humans, but does not explain the mechanism or thresholds behind that decision. Pricing model: No list pricing is published. Arctic Wolf is procured via negotiated AWS Marketplace private offers (consolidated onto the AWS bill), while the in-account ingestion pipeline incurs standard AWS usage charges (estimable via the AWS Pricing Calculator). Prerequisites: Customers must enable AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty and hold an active Arctic Wolf subscription on AWS Marketplace. Teardown & offboarding: Removing the integration requires deleting the CloudFormation stacks (emptying any non-empty S3 buckets first) and notifying the Concierge team beforehand; deleting the stack only stops data ingestion and does not cancel the Marketplace subscription. Key Takeaway I read this article to explore a practical blueprint for security operations: let AI agents shoulder high-volume triage and initial correlation, while keeping business-context decisions firmly in human hands.
Source: Resolve security signals faster with Arctic Wolf’s Aurora Agentic SOC — Tim Sitze, Dan Jellesma, Kent Whitney, AWS Marketplace Blog (October 16, 2026)

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Introduction
content:
Introduction Introduction to Plant Disease Detection The Plant Disease Detection system is designed to provide rapid, accurate, and explainable identification of tomato crop diseases from field images. By bridging modern computer vision research with cloud engineering on AWS, the project provides farmers, agronomists, and researchers with an intuitive web application capable of running CPU-efficient deep learning inference in real-time.
The application accepts standard JPEG or PNG leaf photographs taken from smartphones or cameras, analyzes the visual symptoms using a fine-tuned deep learning model, and outputs ranked disease predictions along with statistical confidence scores.
Classification Scope & Target Classes The underlying neural network is trained to classify images into 11 distinct output classes, covering common bacterial, fungal, and viral infections in tomato leaves, as well as healthy controls and out-of-distribution inputs:
Class ID Disease / Category Name Pathogen / Condition Typical Visual Symptoms 0 Tomato___Bacterial_spot Xanthomonas campestris Small, water-soaked, dark spots with yellow halos 1 Tomato___Early_blight Alternaria solani Concentric target-like dark rings surrounded by chlorosis 2 Tomato___Late_blight Phytophthora infestans Irregular grayish-green water-soaked lesions on leaves 3 Tomato___Leaf_Mold Passalora fulva Pale green or yellow spots on upper surface, velvety olive mold below 4 Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot Septoria lycopersici Numerous circular spots with gray centers and dark margins 5 Tomato___Spider_mites Tetranychus urticae Yellow or white stippling, webbing on leaf undersides 6 Tomato___Target_Spot Corynespora casiicola Brown lesions with prominent concentric rings 7 Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus Geminivirus (Whitefly-borne) Upward curling, severe stunting, and bright interveinal chlorosis 8 Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus Tobamovirus Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns, leaf distortion 9 Tomato___healthy Control / Normal Vigorous green foliage free from chlorosis or necrotic tissue 10 unknown Out-of-Distribution Non-tomato foliage, corrupted images, or background noise [!NOTE] This system serves as a learning, research, and engineering deployment demonstration; field diagnostic certification must be established prior to commercial agronomic use.
Machine Learning Architecture: Knowledge Distillation To balance high predictive accuracy with cost-effective cloud hosting on resource-constrained AWS EC2 CPU instances, the research compared several model architectures and adopted Knowledge Distillation:
flowchart TD Teacher["Teacher Model: ConvNeXt-Tiny<br/>(Heavyweight, High Capacity ~114 MiB)"] Student["Student Model: MobileNetV3-Small<br/>(Lightweight, CPU-Optimized ~6 MiB)"] Data["Tomato Leaf Dataset<br/>(Augmented Preprocessing)"] --> Teacher Data --> Student Teacher -->|Soft Probability Logits| KD_Loss["Knowledge Distillation Loss<br/>(KL Divergence + Cross-Entropy)"] Student -->|Student Predictions| KD_Loss KD_Loss -->|Backprop / Distill Knowledge| DistilledModel["Deployable Checkpoint:<br/>mobilenetv3_small_100_distilled_best.pth<br/>(Latency: 29.23 ms | Size: 6 MiB)"] Teacher Architecture (ConvNeXt-Tiny): Modern convolutional network with inverted bottlenecks, large 7x7 receptive fields, and superior feature extraction capabilities. Student Architecture (MobileNetV3-Small): Hardware-aware network search architecture utilizing hard-swish non-linearities and depthwise separable convolutions, optimized specifically for low-latency CPU execution. Outcome: The distilled MobileNetV3 model retained over 96% of the teacher’s classification capability while reducing model size by over 94% (down to ~6 MiB) and achieving a lightning-fast single-request CPU inference latency of 29.23 ms. Explainable AI (XAI) with Grad-CAM++ A critical requirement in agricultural diagnostics is explainability: agronomists must understand why the model made a specific prediction. The application incorporates Grad-CAM++ (Generalized Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) to generate heatmaps highlighting the exact pixel regions that contributed most strongly to the predicted disease class.
Visual Comparison Across Architectures The following visualizations illustrate how different model architectures focus on distinct pathological features of the leaf:
Architecture Model Role Heatmap & Overlay Visualization MobileNetV3-Small Distilled Production Deployment ConvNeXt-Tiny Teacher Baseline EfficientNet-B0 Candidate Student Operational Pipeline on AWS The operational lifecycle connects code repository automation to AWS infrastructure:
Automated Continuous Delivery: Commits to the master branch in GitHub trigger GitHub Actions workflows that execute Python unit tests, Next.js build verification, and build production container images published to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). Decoupled Checkpoint Storage: Model weights (model.pth) and class label mappings (class_to_idx.json) are maintained in a secure, private Amazon S3 bucket under the prefix mobilenet-distilled-v1/. Containerized EC2 Host: A single Amazon Linux 2023 EC2 instance pulls container images and mounts S3 model artifacts read-only into /app/artifacts. Networking & Ingress: The browser connects to the Next.js frontend on port 3000, which communicates seamlessly with the FastAPI backend on port 8000. Observability: Container standard output and error streams are captured via the Docker awslogs driver into CloudWatch Logs. The CloudWatch Agent collects fine-grained host memory and disk utilization, reporting metrics to automated alarm triggers.

title: Prerequisites & Setup
content:
Prerequisites & Setup Before launching the Plant Disease Detection application on Amazon Web Services, verify the following account permissions, compute infrastructure, and security settings.
Prerequisites & Dependency Matrix The table below summarizes the exact configuration requirements recorded during the deployment:
Dependency Area Required Specification Purpose & Details AWS Account Personal AWS Account Dedicated sandbox environment for demonstration and cost control AWS Region Sydney (ap-southeast-2) Low network latency and full regional availability of EC2, S3, and CloudWatch Compute Engine Amazon EC2 (Amazon Linux 2023 x86_64) Production host running Docker Engine and AWS CLI v2 VPC & Network Public Subnet (0.0.0.0/0 -> Internet Gateway) Direct routing for package updates and inbound web access; Public IPv4 assigned Inbound Security Port 22 (SSH), Port 3000 (Frontend), Port 8000 (API) Restricted strictly to the operator’s approved public IPv4 client address (/32) Model Storage Amazon S3 (Private Bucket) Stores model checkpoints under the mobilenet-distilled-v1/ prefix IAM Instance Role EC2 Instance Profile Grants s3:GetObject on model artifacts and CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy Log Ingestion Role logs:FilterLogEvents Required for operators to tail and query CloudWatch container logs via the AWS CLI Model Artifacts Verified model.pth and class_to_idx.json Release artifacts matched via cryptographic SHA256 checksums [!WARNING] Do NOT use wildcard 0.0.0.0/0 for inbound SSH (port 22) or API management ports. Restrict ingress rules to your specific public IP address to prevent unauthorized intrusion.
Step 1: AWS CLI Configuration & Identity Verification Ensure your operator machine has AWS CLI v2 installed and configured with credentials that have sufficient administrative permissions:
Run the following command to verify your authenticated caller identity and set the active region to Sydney:
# Verify AWS identity aws sts get-caller-identity # Set default region to ap-southeast-2 export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" aws configure set default.region ap-southeast-2 Step 2: EC2 Security Group Inbound Rules Create a dedicated Security Group named plant-disease-sg in your default VPC. Add the following inbound rules:
Type Protocol Port Range Source Description SSH TCP 22 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Administrative SSH shell access Custom TCP TCP 3000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 Next.js Frontend Web Application Custom TCP TCP 8000 <YOUR_CLIENT_IP>/32 FastAPI CPU Inference REST API Step 3: EC2 Instance Profile & IAM Permissions Attach an IAM Role to your EC2 instance so that containers and AWS CLI scripts can securely access Amazon S3 and publish CloudWatch metrics without storing long-lived AWS Access Keys or Secret Keys on the server.
Attach the following IAM policies to the role:
AmazonCloudWatchAgentServerPolicy (AWS Managed Policy): Allows the CloudWatch Agent to emit custom host metrics and create log streams. PlantDiseaseS3Policy (Inline Policy): Grants read-only access strictly to the model artifacts prefix: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AllowS3ModelArtifactsDownload", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2", "arn:aws:s3:::plant-disease-model-artifacts-ap-southeast-2/mobilenet-distilled-v1/*" ] }, { "Sid": "AllowOperatorLogInspection", "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "logs:FilterLogEvents", "logs:GetLogEvents", "logs:DescribeLogStreams" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:logs:ap-southeast-2:*:log-group:/plant-disease/*" } ] } Step 4: Provisioning EC2 Host Software Once logged into your EC2 instance via SSH, install Docker Engine and the CloudWatch Agent:

title: Architecture & Design
content:
Architecture & Design Architectural Principles: Decoupled Weights from Code In standard machine learning operations (MLOps), embedding binary model checkpoints directly into Docker images causes significant operational friction: container images inflate in size, build and push times slow down, and changing a model version forces a complete container rebuild.
The Plant Disease Detection architecture cleanly decouples the code runtime from the model artifacts:
Container Image: Contains only the application logic, dependencies (FastAPI, PyTorch CPU, Next.js), and static assets, keeping the base image compact. Model Storage in Amazon S3: The PyTorch checkpoint (model.pth) and label index dictionary (class_to_idx.json) reside in a private S3 bucket. Runtime Ingestion: During deployment, the EC2 host downloads the target release artifacts using IAM credentials, validates their cryptographic integrity, and mounts them as a read-only volume (/app/artifacts) into the inference container. flowchart TD subgraph S3_Storage ["Amazon S3 (Private Bucket)"] CP["s3://.../mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth (~6 MiB)"] CM["s3://.../mobilenet-distilled-v1/class_to_idx.json"] end subgraph EC2_Host ["Amazon EC2 Instance (ap-southeast-2)"] IAM_Role["EC2 Instance Profile (Role)"] LocalFS["Host Directory: /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1"] subgraph Docker_Runtime ["Docker Container Runtime"] FastAPI["FastAPI Container (:8000)"] NextJS["Next.js Standalone Container (:3000)"] end end IAM_Role -.->|Authorizes aws s3 cp| CP IAM_Role -.->|Authorizes aws s3 cp| CM CP -->|Download & SHA256 Check| LocalFS CM -->|Download & SHA256 Check| LocalFS LocalFS -->|Mount Read-Only into /app/artifacts| FastAPI NextJS -->|HTTP Multipart /predict| FastAPI 5.3.1 Prepare Identity and Artifact Permissions Before initiating file downloads, verify that the EC2 instance has successfully assumed the IAM role and can interact with the S3 regional endpoint:
# Verify instance profile credentials aws sts get-caller-identity # Configure working environment export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="ap-southeast-2" read -r -p "Enter S3 bucket name: " MODEL_BUCKET # Create host directory for model artifacts mkdir -p checkpoints/v1 [!NOTE] The current deployment utilizes S3 regional service endpoints accessed via the public subnet’s default route table to the Internet Gateway. In enterprise production environments with private VPC subnets, an Amazon S3 Gateway VPC Endpoint can be provisioned to route traffic entirely over AWS private network backbones at zero data transfer cost.
5.3.2 Download and Validate Artifacts Execute the following commands to download the release checkpoint and class mapping from Amazon S3, followed by an immediate cryptographic hash verification:
# Download model weights and class index aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/model.pth" checkpoints/v1/model.pth aws s3 cp "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET/mobilenet-distilled-v1/class_to_idx.json" checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json # Verify SHA256 checksums sha256sum checkpoints/v1/model.pth checkpoints/v1/class_to_idx.json Recorded Verification Hashes The downloaded files must match the exact cryptographic digests generated during the offline model training and validation audit:
Artifact File Expected SHA256 Checksum Approximate Size Verification Status model.pth 05e72798a74193499f17c4c8267c1436e8bc65cc1e8b8037245664a17644efa5 ~6.0 MiB MATCHED class_to_idx.json ff5c73e7a7e3e495593fa664b75ebc73de4c9a425f1d847351ae60bc1fbaa786 ~1.2 KiB MATCHED [!IMPORTANT] A mismatch in SHA256 indicates either an incomplete download, an outdated release artifact, or potential tampering. The FastAPI backend refuses to serve traffic and returns an explicit 503 Service Unavailable if weights fail integrity checks.
Model Artifact Explainability Comparison The distilled MobileNetV3-Small weights preserve high fidelity to the ConvNeXt-Tiny teacher while significantly reducing parameter count:
Teacher Model (ConvNeXt-Tiny) Student Model (MobileNetV3-Small Distilled) Broad receptive field capturing overall leaf morphology Concentrated gradient heatmaps targeting necrotic lesion margins

title: Deployment Strategy
content:
Deployment Strategy 5.4.1 Continuous Delivery Pipeline The deployment pipeline is anchored by automated continuous integration (CI) workflows executed on GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/ci.yml). Every commit to the repository triggers:
Python static code analysis, linting, and unit test suites across model transforms and prediction schemas. Next.js production builds, ensuring static asset optimization, TypeScript type safety, and non-root runtime compatibility. Multi-stage Docker image packaging for both the frontend and inference API, followed by automated publishing to GHCR (GitHub Container Registry). Recorded Release Provenance To guarantee reproducibility and avoid mutable tag discrepancies (such as :latest), the deployment recorded immutable git commit hashes and image digests:
Component Target Version / Identifier Recorded Digest Hash Git Commit ff6b75bf3a625db124cc6449f52fa224bf76631e Validated release baseline Backend API Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-api sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c Frontend Image ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-frontend sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.2 Configure Backend Runtime The backend container runs a FastAPI application under Python 3.12 with PyTorch CPU. The host mounts the previously downloaded checkpoints/v1 directory as a read-only volume at /app/artifacts.
Start the backend container with the following configuration:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-api \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 8000:8000 \ -v /home/ec2-user/checkpoints/v1:/app/artifacts:ro \ -e MODEL_CHECKPOINT=/app/artifacts/model.pth \ -e MODEL_CLASS_MAP=/app/artifacts/class_to_idx.json \ -e MODEL_NAME=mobilenetv3_small_100 \ -e MODEL_THREADS=2 \ -e CORS_ORIGINS="http://localhost:3000,http://$(curl -s http://checkip.amazonaws.com):3000" \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/backend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-api@sha256:f61be1570a834f1819614ad041f79e6114e00a0503852a121a564725cad4c27c [!NOTE]
MODEL_THREADS=2 restricts PyTorch intra-op parallelism to 2 CPU cores, preventing inference requests from overwhelming the host OS. The application initializes the neural network weights strictly once at process startup. If weights are missing, corrupt, or incompatible, /health reports status unavailable and API calls return 503. 5.4.3 Configure Frontend and Networking The frontend is packaged using a multi-stage Docker build producing a Next.js Standalone server running on Node.js 20. The container runs as a dedicated non-root nextjs user and listens on port 3000.
Start the frontend container:
docker run -d \ --name plant-disease-frontend \ --restart unless-stopped \ -p 3000:3000 \ -e NODE_ENV=production \ -e PORT=3000 \ --log-driver awslogs \ --log-opt awslogs-region=ap-southeast-2 \ --log-opt awslogs-group=/plant-disease/frontend \ --log-opt awslogs-create-group=true \ ghcr.io/starkkk1/plant-disease-frontend@sha256:ec211d13241680f208b29f8282c7fb12a19735e9048d1f8dab9b6a27499a7f85 5.4.4 Validate Application Behavior Verify that both containers are running healthy, then execute health checks and a test prediction using the fixture leaf image:
# 1. Check running containers sudo docker ps # 2. Check Backend Health curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 3. Check Frontend HTTP Header curl -I http://127.0.0.1:3000 # 4. Perform Live Inference with Fixture Image curl --fail-with-body \ -F "file=@frontend/tests/fixtures/tomato-leaf.jpg;type=image/jpeg" \ -F "top_k=3" \ http://127.0.0.1:8000/predict Recorded Verification Results The table below documents the empirical test results recorded on the Sydney EC2 deployment:

title: Testing & Quality
content:
Testing & Quality 5.5.1 Container Logging & Host Metrics Collection Production observabilty relies on Amazon CloudWatch Logs and the Amazon CloudWatch Agent:
1. Container Structured Logging The Docker daemon uses the awslogs log driver to stream all stdout and stderr output directly to dedicated CloudWatch Log Groups:
/plant-disease/backend: Captures structured JSON middleware access logs, including request_id, client IP, HTTP method, request path, status code, and execution duration. /plant-disease/frontend: Captures Next.js server requests, static file requests, and rendering errors. Log Retention: Set to 7 days to minimize storage overhead while preserving troubleshooting history. Inspect real-time application logs using the AWS CLI:
# Stream the last 10 minutes of backend API logs aws logs tail /plant-disease/backend --since 10m --region ap-southeast-2 # Filter for errors or warnings aws logs filter-log-events \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --filter-pattern "ERROR" \ --region ap-southeast-2 2. CloudWatch Agent Metrics While standard EC2 monitoring provides hypervisor-level CPU utilization, memory and disk metrics are not visible from the hypervisor. The Amazon CloudWatch Agent is configured on the host to collect and report memory and disk telemetry every 60 seconds under the custom namespace PlantDisease/Host:
Create /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json:
{ "metrics": { "namespace": "PlantDisease/Host", "metrics_collected": { "mem": { "measurement": [ "mem_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 }, "disk": { "measurement": [ "disk_used_percent" ], "metrics_collection_interval": 60, "resources": [ "/" ] } } } } Start the CloudWatch Agent service and verify status:
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl \ -a fetch-config -m ec2 -s -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json # Check agent status sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a status 5.5.2 Configure Host RAM Saturation Alarm To protect the single-host deployment from memory exhaustion caused by unexpected traffic surges, configure a CloudWatch Alarm on host memory usage:
Alarm Specification Metric Parameter Target Setting Namespace PlantDisease/Host Metric Name mem_used_percent Statistic Average Evaluation Period 60 seconds (1 minute) Breach Threshold Greater than 85% (> 85) Evaluation Window 3 consecutive periods out of 3 (3 breaching datapoints) Missing Data Treatment Treat missing data as missing Alarm Action Publish notification to SNS topic plant-disease-alerts Create the SNS notification topic and alarm via the AWS CLI:
# 1. Create SNS topic SNS_TOPIC_ARN=$(aws sns create-topic \ --name plant-disease-alerts \ --region ap-southeast-2 \ --query 'TopicArn' --output text) # 2. Subscribe operator email address aws sns subscribe \ --topic-arn "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --protocol email \ --notification-endpoint "your-email@example.com" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 3. Create CloudWatch Metric Alarm aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \ --alarm-name "PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization" \ --alarm-description "Triggers when host memory exceeds 85% for 3 consecutive minutes" \ --namespace "PlantDisease/Host" \ --metric-name "mem_used_percent" \ --statistic Average \ --period 60 \ --threshold 85 \ --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \ --evaluation-periods 3 \ --datapoints-to-alarm 3 \ --alarm-actions "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --region ap-southeast-2 [!TIP] Controlled Testing: To verify email dispatch without artificially exhausting system memory, temporarily lower the alarm threshold to 0% (--threshold 0). Confirm that CloudWatch transitions to the ALARM state and an email arrives in your inbox. Once confirmed, restore the threshold to 85% and verify the alarm returns to OK.
5.5.3 Security Hardening & Least Privilege The architecture adheres strictly to AWS Well-Architected security best practices:
flowchart TD subgraph Security_Best_Practices ["Security Controls Applied"] P1["S3 Private Bucket: Block All Public Access enabled"] P2["IAM Instance Profile: No hardcoded credentials"] P3["Security Group: Ingress locked to operator /32"] P4["Container Isolation: Read-Only volume mounts"] P5["Non-Root Execution: User nextjs & appuser"] end Private S3 Bucket: S3 Block Public Access is completely enabled. Model weights are accessible solely by authenticated requests bearing the EC2 instance’s assumed IAM role. Elimination of Long-Lived Credentials: No access keys, secret keys, or private SSH keys are stored in source control or on the server file system. Read-Only Container Mounts: The model weights directory /app/artifacts is mounted into the container with the :ro flag, ensuring the inference engine cannot mutate model checkpoints. Non-Root Execution: The production container images create and execute under dedicated low-privilege system accounts (nextjs UID 1001 for frontend, appuser for backend).

title: Operations & Cleanup
content:
Operations & Cleanup Daily Operational Routine In a learning, research, or proof-of-concept environment, continuous 24/7 EC2 execution accumulates unnecessary hourly compute costs. Establish a disciplined routine for pausing and resuming workloads:
1. Pausing Applications Between Sessions When halting daily development, pause the container runtime and stop the underlying EC2 instance:
# On EC2 Host via SSH: Gracefully stop application containers sudo docker stop plant-disease-frontend plant-disease-api # From Operator Terminal or AWS CloudShell: Stop the EC2 instance aws ec2 stop-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 [!NOTE] Stopping an EC2 instance halts hourly EC2 compute billing. Attached Amazon EBS root volumes, stored CloudWatch metrics, and S3 objects remain intact but continue to incur standard low-cost storage fees.
2. Resuming Operations When resuming work, restart the instance and initialize services in the correct dependency sequence:
# 1. Start EC2 instance aws ec2 start-instances --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Reconnect via SSH (Note: Public IPv4 may change unless using an Elastic IP) ssh -i key.pem ec2-user@<NEW_PUBLIC_IP> # 3. Start Backend first and await readiness sudo docker start plant-disease-api curl --retry 5 --retry-connrefused http://127.0.0.1:8000/health # 4. Start Frontend sudo docker start plant-disease-frontend [!IMPORTANT] If your EC2 instance does not have an allocated Elastic IP (EIP), stopping and restarting the instance assigns a new public IPv4 address. You must update your SSH connection string, client browser URL, and backend CORS_ORIGINS setting accordingly.
Complete Teardown & Resource Deletion Checklist At the conclusion of the workshop or project lifecycle, execute the following teardown procedure to ensure zero residual billing across your AWS account:
flowchart TD Step1["1. Terminate EC2 Instance<br/>(Automatically deletes attached root EBS volume)"] Step2["2. Delete EBS Snapshots & Unattached Volumes"] Step3["3. Delete CloudWatch Log Groups<br/>(/plant-disease/backend, /plant-disease/frontend)"] Step4["4. Delete CloudWatch Alarm & SNS Topic<br/>(PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization)"] Step5["5. Empty and Delete S3 Bucket Artifacts<br/>(mobilenet-distilled-v1/)"] Step6["6. Release Elastic IP Address (if assigned)"] Step1 --> Step2 --> Step3 --> Step4 --> Step5 --> Step6 Step-by-Step Deletion Commands: # 1. Terminate the EC2 instance aws ec2 terminate-instances \ --instance-ids "$INSTANCE_ID" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 2. Delete CloudWatch Log Groups aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/backend \ --region ap-southeast-2 aws logs delete-log-group \ --log-group-name /plant-disease/frontend \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 3. Delete CloudWatch Alarm aws cloudwatch delete-alarms \ --alarm-names "PlantDisease-HighMemoryUtilization" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 4. Delete SNS Topic aws sns delete-topic \ --topic-arn "$SNS_TOPIC_ARN" \ --region ap-southeast-2 # 5. Empty and delete S3 Bucket aws s3 rm "s3://$MODEL_BUCKET" --recursive aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$MODEL_BUCKET" --region ap-southeast-2 # 6. Release Elastic IP (if allocated) aws ec2 release-address --allocation-id "$EIP_ALLOC_ID" --region ap-southeast-2 References & Documentation The architectural designs, performance benchmarks, and implementation decisions in this workshop adhere to the following technical references:
[1] Project Repository & Release Artifacts: starkkk1/plant-disease-detection — Complete training notebooks, model export scripts, and Next.js / FastAPI source code. [2] AWS EC2 Stop and Start Lifecycle: AWS Documentation on Instance Lifecycle — Details on state preservation, ephemeral storage behavior, and public IP reassignments. [3] Amazon S3 HeadObject and Least-Privilege IAM: S3 Security Best Practices — Policy scoping for model weight downloads and bucket isolation.
